question: The non-consensual sharing of intimate or manipulated material, including content generated or modified using artificial intelligence, constitutes a serious violation of privacy and human dignity that affects women and young people in particular. Recent incidents and pending court cases in Member States, including Greece, highlight risks of repeated victim exposure.

Despite Directive (EU) 2024/1385, Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), there are still shortcomings in the protection of victims and in ensuring their dignity in the legal process. The need for systematic European intervention remains urgent. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What additional actions does it consider necessary to enhance the safety, dignity and protection of personal data of victims of online gender-based violence?

How does the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) ensure respect for the principle of proportionality and prevent secondary victimisation during the processing of sensitive data in its use as evidence?

What monitoring mechanisms and procedures are in place to ensure the uniform and effective implementation of Directive (EU) 2024/1385 in the Member States, with a view to effectively protecting the dignity and safety of victims?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.6.2026) Under the Victims’ Rights Directive1, Member States must ensure that competent authorities protect victims’ privacy during criminal proceedings, including their personal characteristics and images of victims and of their family members.
The processing of personal data of victims of online gender-based violence (GBV) by law enforcement authorities in criminal investigations falls within the scope of Directive (EU) 2016/6802.

Directive (EU) 2024/13853 (the Violence Against Women (VAW) Directive) further protects the dignity of victims of online GBV by criminalising the most serious forms of cyberviolence and providing for protection and support measures. It requires the rapid removal of illegal content, safeguards personal data in investigations and court proceedings, and recognises these harms as violations of fundamental rights4.

Member States must transpose the VAW Directive by 14 June 2027. This will strengthen the role of the Digital Services Act5, whose provisions will apply to cybercrimes as defined in Articles 5 to 8 of the VAW Directive, which will be considered illegal content. The VAW Directive also requires the Commission to evaluate its impact and assess whether its scope or measures should be expanded6.

The Commission supports Member States in the transposition of the VAW Directive to promote timely and correct transposition. If Member States fail to fulfil their implementation obligations, the Commission will not hesitate to launch infringement procedures, as appropriate.

Furthermore, in the context of the Omnibus on AI, the EU co-legislators have agreed on the need to introduce into the AI Act7 a prohibition of AI systems that generate or manipulate non-consensual intimate content of identifiable natural persons.
